episode.title: Marine Biology for Divers
episode.description: What divers often misidentify, how reefs recover, and how to be a better observer without touching anything.

feed.description: Scuba diving stories and skills: safety, marine life, travel, and calm thinking underwater.
feed.title: Below the Surface

bullets: Coral bleaching events are not random — they are driven by predictable environmental stressors that reveal underlying system vulnerabilities.
Most reef damage from divers stems from anchor strikes rather than fin contact, a critical distinction often overlooked in dive operations.
Erosion in coastal areas drives sediment plumes that degrade reef ecosystems — a failure mode that becomes visible when teams adopt PADI-certified practices.
The framing of a problem determines which trade-offs are made — for example, how dive tooling is selected influences the visibility of second-order effects.
Using Suunto-class tooling outside of standard frameworks makes the failure mode harder to detect, leading to repeated rebuilding efforts down the line.
Shark dives reveal a shift in perspective: the real issue is not the dive itself but the assumptions embedded in how it's framed.
Soil erosion is a cross-cutting factor — its impacts on reef health are systemic and interwoven with other conservation challenges.
The key heuristic is internalizing that coral bleaching is not stochastic — once this is accepted, decision-making becomes more coherent and effective.
